author: inventshah
text:
You may want tokenize-rt.

The stdlib tokenize module does not properly roundtrip. This wrapper around the stdlib provides two additional tokens ESCAPED_NL and UNIMPORTANT_WS, and a Token data type. Use src_to_tokens and tokens_to_src to roundtrip.
This library is useful if you’re writing a refactoring tool based on the python tokenization.

author: NickC
aroberge
text:
@inventshah mentions using tokenize-rt. Another option is to use token-utils which also guarantees perfect round-trip.  Adapting your code to use token-utils:
from token_utils import tokenize, untokenize

source_code = """
if True:
    # comment one <- gets incorrectly dedented, indent doesn't happen until after this line
    x = 1
# comment two -> gets incorrectly indented, dedent doesn't happen until after this line
x = 2
# comment three
"""
modi_toks = []
toks = tokenize(source_code)

for tok in toks:
    modi_toks.append(tok)
modi_source = untokenize(modi_toks)

assert modi_source == source_code

In addition, since you want to modify the source code, tokens from token-utils are mutable.

author: jrivers
text:
A line with a comment by itself does not actually need to be correctly indented, so the tokenizer is right to not emit INDENT/DEDENT tokens there.
For example:
if True:
# should the INDENT still come before the comment here?
    pass

if True:
        # where should the INDENT be emitted in this case?
    pass

It’s fine for the comment to go anywhere on the line, so these examples are both correct.

text: Based on the usage guide tokens_to_src takes an iterable of Token objects not of tuples. Did you try modi_toks.append(tok) instead? You can modify the token objects too. tokenize-rt is specifically not a direct API compatible drop-in for tokenize.

author: aroberge
text:
Tokens from token-utils are NOT two-tuples and cannot be replaced by two-tuples.
The documentation, and in particular the “recipes”, should have all that you need to find out how to modify a token stream. In particular, if you simply want to append a new token, you can append a simple string.

author: aroberge
text:
Nick:

Just had a go at removing some tokens but, unless I am missing something obvious, they are getting added back in again


As shown in some examples in the documentation, to remove a token, simply set its string to the empty string: tok.string = ''; alternatively, as mentioned in untokenizing  … If you don’t want to set a token’s string to the empty string to effectively remove it, and absolutely want to remove a token, then use stringify() instead of untokenize() to obtain a string version; note however that all token characters will be replaced by spaces.
In the link above, you will find the explanation as to why attempting to remove a token and use untokenize() does not produce the expected result.

author: inventshah
text: src_to_tokens returns a list of tokens, so you can append, insert, and remove as if it was a normal list. Since Token is a namedtuple, you can use ._replace() to edit fields, or simply construct a new Token as desired. I suggest experimenting, perhaps with assistance of an LLM. Both tokenize-rt and the token-utils libraries seem to support what you’d like and have numerous examples linked in their corresponding guides.

Build your proof of concept with whatever dependencies you need. Once it is ready and fully explained, people will be able to see what you have made. So far (afaik) we haven’t seen even a simple example of what your preprocessor will be able to do, what problems it will solve, and what power it will provide.
A working tool with some documentation will explain your idea. Then people can use the tool, and you might have others helping you argue your case for making a change to Python itself. Minimizing dependencies shouldn’t be your top priority. Explaining your vision should be.
